01

Start with this: it is a folder, not an app

The single idea that makes everything else make sense.

Nothing in this project runs on a server.

The repository is a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images. GitHub Pages takes whatever is sitting on the main branch and publishes that folder to the web, exactly as it is. When a student opens a lesson, their browser downloads those files and assembles the page on their own laptop. There is no database, no login, no backend to break at 8:05 in the morning.

Two consequences follow from that, and they explain most of the rules in CLAUDE.md.

First: what is on main is what students have. There is no staging environment between you and the classroom. That is why a test suite runs before every push, and why the branch protection rule exists.

Second: the same file has to serve 77 lessons. Rather than 77 hand-built pages, this repo has one renderer and 77 small data files. Fix a bug in the renderer once and all 71 unit lessons are fixed. That leverage is the whole design, and it is also why hand-editing a generated file is treated as an error rather than a shortcut.

02

How a change reaches a student

Seven stages, three of them on your laptop and four on GitHub.

This is the loop you will run hundreds of times. Everything in the diagram below is automatic except the four moments where you type a command.

The one thing to internalise: a commit is not a save and a push is not a publish. Committing writes a snapshot into your local history and touches nothing on the internet. Pushing sends those snapshots to GitHub. Only stage 6, moving main, changes what students see.

The fastest way to stop feeling lost in a repository is to stop reading it as a list of folders and start reading it as a small number of roles. This one has five, and the arrows between them run in a single direction.

04

Anatomy of one lesson

Open a lesson file and you will find almost nothing in it. That is intentional.

unit-1/lesson-1-1-song-china.html is about 5 KB. It has no lecture, no checkpoints, no images. It is a frame with empty containers and three script tags. Everything a student reads arrives from three other files at load time.

The ten modules, always in this order

Every lesson page shows exactly ten module cards, no more and no fewer. Eight of them open a pop-out. One is a jump link down the page. One opens an external simulation in a new tab.

  • 01Map & GeographyPop-out. Needs a real map image.
  • 02First & 10 ReadingPop-out. Embeds the capture wrapper.
  • 03Content DeliveryJump link only, never a pop-out.
  • 04BeSurrealPop-out. Required in every data file.
  • 05AP Skill BuilderPop-out. Feeds the Skills Lens.
  • 06Checkpoint 1Pop-out. Terms feed skills-map.js.
  • 07Evidence LabPop-out. Images must be buttons.
  • 08Primary SourcePop-out. Socrates AI Coach in Foundations.
  • 09BeInTheRoomExternal link, or a coming soon card.
  • 10Checkpoint 2Pop-out. The last thing they write.
05

Where the readings come from

All 77 First & 10 readings are generated. None of them are hand-written any more.

This is the part that trips people up, because the readings look like ordinary HTML pages sitting in unit-3/. They are outputs. The words live in three Node modules under scripts/lib/, and one template turns them into pages.

06

Where student work goes

There is no server, so the path is unusual, and worth knowing exactly.

Because nothing runs on a server, student writing cannot be posted anywhere by the page itself. It is held in the browser, gathered into one block by the lesson page, and carried into Canvas by the student. Canvas is the only channel. The Google Form was retired in August and validate.js now fails the build if any part of it reappears.

08

What is protecting you

Three layers, each catching what the one before it cannot see.

LayerWhenWhat it catches
Pre-push hookEvery push, about 5 secondsRuns npm test. Structure, capture wiring, image integrity, and the reproducibility checks. If it fails, the push never happens.
Validate workflowEvery push, on GitHubTwo jobs. structure runs with no install at all, which is what keeps the offline suite honestly dependency free. browser installs Chromium and runs the seven interaction tests.
Nightly workflowOvernightChecks every remote Wikimedia image URL still resolves. It sits off the push path on purpose, because someone else's outage must never fail your commit.

Exit code 2 means skipped, not passed. Every browser test exits 2 when playwright-core is missing, because validate.js has to stay runnable on a bare checkout. Locally that is fine and reported as SKIP. In CI both workflows pass --strict, which turns a skip into a failure, so a green browser job can never mean it ran nothing.

Worth knowing what none of these can see: a scroll lock, a colour contrast failure, a modal that traps a keyboard user. Structural checks stayed green through the whole lecture deck bug that left students unable to scroll. That is why the browser suite exists, and why it asserts the page really scrolls rather than only that a flag was cleared.

09

The words GitHub uses

Defined against this repository, rather than in the abstract.

Repository
The folder, plus its entire history. Your copy on this laptop is a full repository, not a view of one on a server. That is why git log works with no internet.
Working tree
The files as they are on disk right now, including edits you have not committed. git status tells you what has changed here.
Commit
A permanent, named snapshot of the whole repository at one moment, with a message saying why. Commits are cheap and safe. Make them often.
Branch
A movable label pointing at one commit. main is a branch. Your working branch is another. Switching branches swaps the whole folder to that snapshot.
origin
The nickname for the copy on GitHub. git push -u origin my-branch means: send my commits to the copy called origin, and remember that pairing.
Push and pull
Push sends commits up to GitHub. Pull brings commits down. Neither one runs anything or changes the live site by itself.
Fast-forward
Moving a branch label forward to a commit that is already ahead of it, with no new commit made. This is how main is updated here: it is pointed at a commit that already passed CI, so the tested thing and the shipped thing are the same object.
GitHub Actions
GitHub's robot. It reads .github/workflows/*.yml and runs those steps on a fresh machine every time you push. The Validate workflow is what turns a commit green or red.
GitHub Pages
The free web host that serves this repository's main branch as a website. It publishes files, it does not run code.
Hook
A script git runs at a set moment. This repo has one pre-push hook, in .githooks/, and npm install points git at it. Override once with git push --no-verify, and only when you know why.
Ruleset
A protection rule on a branch. The one in .github/branch-ruleset.json makes main undeletable, unforceable, and closed to any commit that has not passed both Validate jobs.
10

The five commands

Everything else has an npm alias you can look up in package.json when you need it.

  • git statusWhat have I changed, and which branch am I on. Run it before and after everything until it becomes reflex.
  • npm run serveOpen the site locally and click through it like a student, before anyone else sees it.
  • npm testThe gate. About five seconds. It is what the hook and CI both run, so a green here is a green there.
  • git add -A && git commit -m "..."Take the snapshot. Write the message for the version of you who reads it in March.
  • git push -u origin <branch>Send it to GitHub, where Validate picks it up. Nothing reaches students until main moves.

If you only remember one habit

Small commits, pushed to a working branch, with npm test green. Everything in this repository is recoverable from a commit. Nothing is recoverable from an edit you never committed.
